lesson.title: Stimulus Discrimination: Learning Which Stimuli Actually Matter
lesson.summary: Stimulus discrimination is the learned ability to respond to a specific conditioned stimulus while not responding to other, similar stimuli that have never actually predicted the unconditioned stimulus.
lesson.body:
Generalization lets an organism respond broadly to anything resembling a learned stimulus, but that broad response is not always useful. Discrimination is the corrective process: through further experience, an organism learns to tell the difference between the true conditioned stimulus and other stimuli that merely resemble it, responding only to the one that has actually been associated with the unconditioned stimulus.

Pavlov produced discrimination in his dogs through what is sometimes called differential reinforcement of different tones. If a dog had begun generalizing salivation to a range of tones, Pavlov could narrow that response back down by consistently pairing food only with the original training tone while presenting the similar tones without food. Over repeated trials, salivation to the food paired tone stayed strong while salivation to the other tones faded. The dog had learned to discriminate.

Discrimination and generalization work as a pair, and both are shaped by consequences. An animal that generalizes too broadly wastes energy responding to irrelevant stimuli, while one that discriminates too narrowly might miss real signals. Real learning tends to settle somewhere in between, refined by which stimuli actually keep predicting something meaningful and which do not. This same logic, responding differently depending on what a stimulus has actually been shown to predict, resurfaces later in operant conditioning as well, where organisms learn to behave differently depending on the situation they are in.
